summary.text: The counterexample is $n=800{,}322{,}180$: monotonicity of $\binom{2k+1}{k}$ and $\binom{33}{16}>n$ reduce the possibilities to $0\le c\le d\le15$. A finite check of these pairs shows that every remainder $n-\binom{2c+1}{c}-\binom{2d+1}{d}$ either has a prime $p\equiv3\pmod4$ dividing it but not $p^2$, or is $2^v t$ with $t\equiv3\pmod4$, so none is a sum of two squares.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
B(k)=\binom{2k+1}{k}
\]
and put
\[
N=800{,}322{,}180.
\]
We will prove that there are no nonnegative integers \(a,b,c,d\), even without imposing \(a\le b\), such that \(c\le d\) and
\[
N=a^2+b^2+B(c)+B(d).
\]
It will follow that the number of representations counted by A303639 is zero at \(N\), which disproves the assertion that it is positive for every integer greater than 1.

We first record two elementary obstructions to being a sum of two squares.

**Lemma 1 (the power-of-two obstruction).** If
\[
m=2^v t\qquad\text{with}\qquad t\equiv3\pmod4,
\]
then \(m\) is not a sum of two integer squares.

Indeed, a square is congruent to either 0 or 1 modulo 4, so a number congruent to 3 modulo 4 cannot be a sum of two squares. It remains to observe that if \(2k=x^2+y^2\), then \(k\) is itself a sum of two squares. Since \(x^2+y^2\) is even, \(x\) and \(y\) have the same parity. If they are both even, then
\[
k=2\left((x/2)^2+(y/2)^2\right)
  =\left(x/2+y/2\right)^2+\left(x/2-y/2\right)^2.
\]
If they are both odd, then \((x+y)/2\) and \((x-y)/2\) are integers and
\[
k=\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)^2+\left(\frac{x-y}{2}\right)^2.
\]
(The sign of the second integer is irrelevant after squaring.) Thus a representation of \(2^v t\) as two squares could be divided by 2 in this sense \(v\) times, producing a representation of \(t\). This is impossible because \(t\equiv3\pmod4\).

**Lemma 2 (the odd-prime obstruction).** Let \(p\) be a prime with \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). If \(p\mid m\) but \(p^2\nmid m\), then \(m\) is not a sum of two integer squares.

To prove this, suppose that \(m=x^2+y^2\). Modulo \(p\), we have \(x^2\equiv-y^2\). If \(y\not\equiv0\pmod p\), division by \(y^2\) would show that \(-1\) is a square modulo \(p\). But this is impossible for a prime congruent to 3 modulo 4: if \(z^2\equiv-1\pmod p\), then Fermat's theorem gives
\[
1\equiv z^{p-1}=(z^2)^{(p-1)/2}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\equiv-1\pmod p,
\]
because \((p-1)/2\) is odd. Hence \(y\equiv0\pmod p\), and then \(x^2\equiv0\pmod p\), so primality of \(p\) gives \(x\equiv0\pmod p\) as well. Consequently \(p^2\mid x^2+y^2=m\), contrary to the hypothesis.

We next reduce the possible binomial indices to a finite set. The function \(B(k)\) is nondecreasing. This follows twice from Pascal's identity:
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(k)&=\binom{2k+1}{k}\\
&\le \binom{2k+1}{k}+\binom{2k+1}{k+1}
 =\binom{2k+2}{k+1}\\
&\le \binom{2k+2}{k}+\binom{2k+2}{k+1}
 =\binom{2k+3}{k+1}=B(k+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Direct evaluation of the required binomial coefficients gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
k&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
B(k)&1&3&10&35&126&462&1716&6435
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
k&8&9&10&11&12&13&14&15\\ \hline
B(k)&24310&92378&352716&1352078&5200300&20058300&77558760&300540195.
\end{array}
\]
Also,
\[
B(16)=\binom{33}{16}=1{,}166{,}803{,}110>N.
\]
These values may be obtained directly from the factorial formula for binomial coefficients (or successively from the standard binomial recurrences).

Suppose now, for contradiction, that
\[
N=a^2+b^2+B(c)+B(d),\qquad c\le d.
\]
All four terms on the right are nonnegative, so \(B(d)\le N\). If \(d\ge16\), monotonicity would give
\[
B(d)\ge B(16)=1{,}166{,}803{,}110>N,
\]
a contradiction. Hence
\[
0\le c\le d\le15.
\]
There are therefore exactly \(16\cdot17/2=136\) possible pairs \((c,d)\). For each such pair set
\[
M_{c,d}=N-B(c)-B(d).
\]
The proposed representation would imply
\[
M_{c,d}=a^2+b^2.
\]
We now exclude all 136 possibilities by Lemma 1 or Lemma 2.

Here is the complete arithmetic certificate. Row \(c\) lists its entries in order for
\[
d=c,c+1,\ldots,15.
\]
An entry \(2_v\) means that
\[
M_{c,d}=2^v t\quad\text{with}\quad t\equiv3\pmod4;
\]
thus Lemma 1 applies. An odd entry \(p\) means that \(p\) is a prime satisfying
\[
p\equiv3\pmod4,\qquad p\mid M_{c,d},\qquad p^2\nmid M_{c,d};
\]
thus Lemma 2 applies.

\[
\begin{array}{c|llllllllllllllll}
c=0&647&163&67&2_5&23&467&2_0&2_5&7&3&2_0&3&2_0&2_0&2_0&2_5\\
c=1&2_1&2_0&2_1&2_0&2_0&3&2_1&2_0&2_0&3&2_0&11&3&3&2_1\\
c=2&2_4&2_0&2_2&2_2&2_1&2_0&19&3&2_1&2_2&2_1&2_1&2819&2_0\\
c=3&2_1&2_0&2_0&43&2_1&2_0&2_0&7&2_0&3&23&23&2_1\\
c=4&3&2_3&719&2_0&563&2_2&7&2_3&7&3&2_1&2_0\\
c=5&7&3&2_0&2_6&2_2&3&7&7&3&2_1&2_0\\
c=6&2_2&19&7&2_1&3&139&227&11&7&67\\
c=7&2_1&2_0&2_0&31&2_0&139&3&3&2_1\\
c=8&2_3&3&223&3&59&11&2_1&2_0\\
c=9&19&2_1&2_2&2_1&2_1&19&2_0\\
c=10&2_2&19&2_2&2_2&19&19\\
c=11&7&3&19&2_1&2_0\\
c=12&2_2&2_2&2_4&19\\
c=13&2_2&2_5&3\\
c=14&3&3\\
c=15&2_1
\end{array}
\]

For completeness, this table is obtained simply by subtracting the displayed binomial values from \(N\) and repeatedly dividing by 2 or by the indicated odd prime. The odd primes occurring in the table are
\[
3,7,11,19,23,31,43,59,67,139,163,223,227,467,563,647,719,2819.
\]
Each is congruent to 3 modulo 4, and trial division by primes not exceeding its square root establishes primality. For every odd-prime cell, one division of \(M_{c,d}\) by the displayed prime has zero remainder, while division of the resulting quotient by that prime has nonzero remainder. For every \(2_v\) cell, exactly \(v\) factors of 2 are removed and the remaining quotient has remainder 3 modulo 4. Thus the table records precisely the hypotheses needed by the two lemmas, not merely a search for possible squares.

A few cells illustrate explicitly how the certificate is read. For \((c,d)=(0,0)\),
\[
M_{0,0}=800{,}322{,}180-1-1=800{,}322{,}178
          =647\cdot1{,}236{,}974.
\]
The quotient \(1{,}236{,}974\) is not divisible by 647, so 647 occurs to exact exponent one; moreover \(647\equiv3\pmod4\). Hence Lemma 2 excludes this cell. For \((c,d)=(0,3)\),
\[
M_{0,3}=800{,}322{,}180-1-35
       =800{,}322{,}144
       =2^5\cdot25{,}010{,}067,
\]
and \(25{,}010{,}067\equiv3\pmod4\), so Lemma 1 applies. For the less immediate large-prime entry in row 2, corresponding to \((c,d)=(2,14)\),
\[
M_{2,14}=800{,}322{,}180-10-77{,}558{,}760
        =722{,}763{,}410
        =2819\cdot256{,}390,
\]
and 2819 does not divide 256,390. Since 2819 is prime and \(2819\equiv3\pmod4\), Lemma 2 applies. As an endpoint check, for \((c,d)=(15,15)\),
\[
M_{15,15}=800{,}322{,}180-2(300{,}540{,}195)
=199{,}241{,}790=2\cdot99{,}620{,}895,
\]
with \(99{,}620{,}895\equiv3\pmod4\), matching the final entry \(2_1\).

The triangular layout contains one cell for each \((c,d)\) with \(0\le c\le d\le15\). In every cell, either Lemma 1 or Lemma 2 proves that \(M_{c,d}\) is not a sum of two squares. Therefore no nonnegative \(a,b,c,d\) with \(c\le d\) can satisfy
\[
800{,}322{,}180
=a^2+b^2+\binom{2c+1}{c}+\binom{2d+1}{d}.
\]
In particular there is no such representation satisfying the additional required condition \(a\le b\). Consequently
\[
a(800{,}322{,}180)=0.
\]
Since \(800{,}322{,}180>1\), this is a counterexample to the conjecture that \(a(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>1\).
